title: Korea’s semiconductor recovery offers little protection against a weaker won
summary: Governor Chang Yong Rhee entered 2026 expecting Korean growth to return close to its potential rate and inflation to stay near target. Those forecasts gave little indication of how difficult the next policy decision could be. Semiconductor strength lifted aggregate growth while domestic-oriented firms remained exposed to expensive imports. A weak won could raise inflation even with subdued domestic demand. Renewed pressure on Seoul-area housing added a financial-stability constraint. The governor’s message was conditional: incoming evidence on the exchange rate, housing and the breadth of recovery could pull the Board in different directions. His address announced no Base Rate decision (pp. 1, 3–6).

The previous year illustrated how quickly the ranking of risks could change. Political disruption contributed to negative first-quarter growth. US tariffs in April compounded the uncertainty, which partly receded after the June presidential election and the October APEC meeting. During the first half, slower activity and stable inflation made room for two rate cuts. Vulnerable borrowers also received targeted support through the Bank Intermediated Lending Support Facility. By the second half, Seoul metropolitan housing instability and volatile exchange rates had become sufficiently important for the Bank to keep its rate unchanged. A subsequent recovery in growth could therefore coexist with continued weakness among firms that had benefited from support (pp. 1–2, 6).

The contrast is visible in the November outlook cited in the speech. The Bank projected 1.8% growth in 2026 after 1.0% in 2025. Excluding IT, the projected rate was only 1.4%. Rhee identified trade-policy developments, the semiconductor cycle and the recovery of domestic demand as separate sources of forecast error. Consumer inflation had risen into the low-to-mid 2% range as adverse weather and won depreciation affected prices. The Bank projected 2.1% inflation for 2026, unchanged from the preceding year, assuming temporary pressures eased and demand remained subdued. A prolonged period of exchange-rate weakness could invalidate that assumption. Households also faced the cumulative increase in the price level since the pandemic; achieving a stable inflation rate would leave that burden in place. Rhee cited distribution reform and greater import openness as possible responses where individual prices remained unusually high (pp. 3–4).

Currency flows mattered independently of the domestic policy rate. Rhee considered the late-2025 exchange rate in the upper KRW 1,400s per US dollar substantially out of line with economic fundamentals, while acknowledging the difficulty of identifying a fair level. Korea’s net external creditor position helped distinguish this episode from earlier crises. Growth and interest-rate differentials and the discount on Korean assets contributed, but resident purchases of foreign securities could also create a near-term imbalance. The national pension fund’s predictable foreign purchases and hedges risked encouraging others to anticipate the same depreciation. During market strain the fund could end up buying the dollars that the authorities were selling. A rise in the won value of its foreign assets would then say little about a lasting gain in retirement wealth. A government task force and interagency discussions offered scope for more flexible hedging, with details still to be settled (pp. 4–5).

The upper limit of USD 20 billion per year on US-bound strategic investment was another potential source of mispricing. The agreement left the amount and implementation dependent on FX-market stability. The ceiling alone could not supply a forecast for actual dollar demand. Abroad, fiscal pressures and the role of nonbanks in repo markets made spillovers from higher global long yields worth monitoring. An AI-equity correction raised a different issue: Korean semiconductor manufacturers could remain relatively resilient across competing technology firms, while Korean residents holding the global equities could take losses. The speech offered no estimates of the size or covariance of those exposures (pp. 2–3).

Rhee envisaged more explicit communication about Board members’ conditional three-month rate views, even where explaining a change in conditions might produce immediate rate volatility. He also distinguished the aggregate stance from temporary support for regional SMEs, and envisaged broader collateral arrangements for banks’ loans. Extension to nonbank deposit-taking institutions still required consultation on legislative change. Further work on tokenised deposits, won stablecoins and the Bank’s own language model belonged to its longer-horizon infrastructure agenda. For portfolios, the near-term analytical test is whether FX pressure, sectoral weakness and housing risks move together. The speech gives no market-implied rate path against which to measure the surprise from such a change (pp. 5–8).

questions.question: How persistent would won weakness need to be to put the 2.1% inflation projection at risk?
questions.detail: Rhee identifies the currency as the source of an adverse inflation surprise even if demand stays subdued. He provides no pass-through coefficient or timetable. A front-end rates view depends on whether import-cost increases remain concentrated in a few goods or spread into consumer prices. Start with the November Bank of Korea Economic Outlook cited in the speech and compare exchange-rate assumptions with the import-price and CPI components available at the time.

questions.question: How much dollar demand comes from scheduled purchases, and how much can change with the exchange rate?
questions.detail: The bilateral investment ceiling and the pension fund’s currency hedges represent distinct possible flows. Their disclosure alone supplies little information on net executed dollar demand. Estimating the pressure under stress would require the investment memorandum cited on page 2, pension allocation and hedge disclosures, and balance-of-payments data, with transaction flows separated from valuation changes. This distinction matters to an investor considering whether a currency move can reverse without a policy-rate change.

questions.question: Does semiconductor growth reach domestic borrowers before housing limits the scope for easing?
questions.detail: The gap between headline and ex-IT growth suggests uneven exposure, but the speech gives no transmission estimate from chip exports to wages, credit demand or regional SME cash flows. Examine sectoral production, payrolls and business-lending surveys alongside the November outlook and Seoul-area housing data. Evidence of broadening income growth would change how much weight to place on weak sentiment when interpreting the next Board communication.

limitation: The Bank labels the English text an unofficial translation of the Korean speech.
